cards.explanation: The answer is son, friends. The writer says Abraham was ready to offer his one and only son on the altar. This is the man who had received the promises, so the stakes couldn't be higher. I think this one hurts, so I'll say it once and let it sit.

The answer is that he reasoned God could raise the dead, friends. The promise says Isaac and the test says Isaac, and Abraham lands on this: “Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead…” The writer adds that in a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death.

The answer is True, friends. The writer says Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead. Then comes the line: “…in a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death.” Notice those words, 'in a sense.' I'll keep them right where the writer put them.

The answer is that he worships. Jacob blessed each of Joseph's sons and worshiped as he leaned on the top of his staff. He's dying, he's leaning on a staff, and he's still worshiping. I can barely get through a morning without leaning on the counter and complaining.

The answer is the exodus of the Israelites, friends. With his end near, Joseph spoke about it. Most of us use our last words to ask where the good oven mitts went. This man is looking at the whole future of a people.
The answer is False, friends. The text says “…they were unafraid of the king’s edict.” By faith Moses' parents hid him for three months after his birth. They saw that he was a beautiful child.

The answer is False, friends. The text says Moses “…chose to suffer oppression with God’s people rather than to experience the fleeting enjoyment of sin.” So he went with God's people, not with the enjoyment. That word 'fleeting' says it all. He picked the hard seat with God's people over the comfy one that doesn't last.

The answer is reward, friends. The writer says Moses valued disgrace for Christ above the treasures of Egypt “…for he was looking ahead to his reward.” He wasn't just gritting his teeth. He was looking ahead.

The answer is that he saw the God no one can see. The writer says Moses “…persevered because he saw Him who is invisible.” That's what carried him when he left Egypt, not fearing the king's anger. Keep that line close, friends.

The answer is True, friends. By faith Moses kept the Passover and the sprinkling of blood, “…so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch Israel’s own firstborn.” The writer puts those two things right next to that result. That's the whole point of the verse.

The answer is dry, friends. The writer says by faith the people passed through the Red Sea “…as on dry land…” Think about that: a whole sea, and they crossed it as on dry land. That's a sentence worth reading twice.

The answer is False. By faith the people passed through the Red Sea as on dry land, “but when the Egyptians tried to follow, they were drowned.” The Egyptians did not make it across. That's a heavy line, and the writer states it plainly.

The answer is that they marched around them. The walls of Jericho fell by faith, “…after the people had marched around them for seven days.” No battering ram in the verse, friends. Just a lot of walking and a lot of faith.

The answer is that she welcomed them in peace. Rahab, the prostitute, is on this list because by faith she did not perish with those who were disobedient. The writer says that was “…because she welcomed the spies in peace…” Notice who's on the list, friends. It's a bigger table than you'd guess.

The answer is time, friends. The writer says, “Time will not allow me to tell of Gideon…” and keeps going down the list. He's got more names than he's got room. I know the feeling, because I've run out of rack space for cookies more than once.
The answer is that they shut the mouths of lions, friends. The writer lists it right alongside conquering kingdoms and administering justice. And all of it is through faith.

The answer is fire, friends. The verse says they “…quenched the raging fire…” Then it adds that they escaped the edge of the sword. I get nervous when my oven runs a little hot, so I'm tipping my hat to them.

The answer is True, friends. The writer says these people of faith “…gained strength from weakness…” That line sits right between escaping the edge of the sword and becoming mighty in battle. Honestly, that gives me some hope.

The answer is so they might gain a better resurrection. That's the reason the writer gives: others were tortured and refused their release “…so that they might gain a better resurrection.” I think this is one of the heaviest parts of the whole chapter. So I'll slow down here, friends, and just say it plainly.

The answer is False, and the flip matters. The writer says, “The world was not worthy of them.” They wandered in deserts and mountains, and hid in caves and holes in the ground. Even so, the writer says it is the world that fell short of them.

The answer is something better for us. Hebrews 11:40 says, “God had planned something better for us…” After that long list of faith, that line lands like the smell of fresh cookies coming out of the oven. It means we're part of it, friends.

The answer is True, friends. The writer says God planned something better for us, “…so that together with us they would be made perfect.” Together is the word. All those names on the list, and us too, in the same line.
